elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience.
elements.evidence: New Subparagraph 18.1A: "the Customer may terminate this Agreement or its participation in this Agreement for convenience at any time, including during the Initial Period" — an unconditional Customer election, expressly overriding the 18.1 lock-in via "Notwithstanding Subparagraph 18.1"; "or its participation in this Agreement" is the consortium analogue of an Order Form.

elements.element: Customer's convenience termination requires no more than 30 days' written notice.
elements.evidence: 18.1A: "upon not less than thirty (30) days' prior written notice to the other Parties" — the required notice period is thirty days (a floor on how early Customer must notify, not a ceiling of more than 30 days), so the requirement imposed on Customer does not exceed 30 days.

elements.element: Vendor refunds prepaid fees pro rata after Customer's convenience termination.
elements.evidence: 18.1A: "the other Parties shall refund to the Customer, pro rata, any amounts prepaid by it in respect of the period after the effective date of such termination" — express "pro rata" wording (not merely inferred from a post-termination period), payable by the counterparties; "amounts prepaid" subsumes prepaid fees.

elements.element: Vendor has no right to terminate for convenience during a committed term.
elements.evidence: Retained 18.1 confines any other Party's unilateral withdrawal to "the end of the Initial Period or any time thereafter by giving not less than one (1) year's prior notice"; 18.2 permits mid-term termination only by unanimous written agreement or a 90% Management Committee majority on retirement of APCN 2, which is a collective governance decision, not a unilateral counterparty convenience right. Element was already met and correctly left un-redrafted; 18.1A grants the new right only to the defined Customer, so no new counterparty exit is created.

elements.element: Customer may terminate for convenience on 60 to 90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: 18.1A sets "not less than thirty (30) days' prior written notice", which is below the 60–90 day fallback band (the preferred, better position is taken instead).

elements.element: Any early-termination fee is capped at three months of fees.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: no early-termination fee or exit charge is imposed on Customer anywhere in paragraph 18 as rendered; the only money mechanic retained ("No credit for capital costs will be made to a Party that terminates its participation in accordance with Subparagraph 18.1") is keyed to 18.1 and is not a fee on a 18.1A withdrawal.

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: 18.1 permits a Party's unilateral withdrawal only "at the end of the Initial Period or any time thereafter", i.e. at or after natural term end, not mid-term.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 90 days' notice of convenience termination.
elements.evidence: 18.1 requires "not less than one (1) year's prior notice", exceeding the 90-day floor.

reasons: Preferred level is position-complete: the inserted 18.1A supplies the Customer convenience right, the 30-day notice, and the express pro-rata refund of prepaid amounts, while retained 18.1/18.2 already deny any counterparty a unilateral mid-term convenience exit.

Fallback level is incomplete only on the notice-band element (30 days rather than 60–90), which is immaterial because the stronger preferred level is fully met; the comment properly offers the fallback as an alternative rather than relying on it.

Minimality holds: the redline is a single concise insertion for a missing Customer exit, with no deletions, no survival tail, no at-own-expense or extra-damages language, and no re-drafting of the already-acceptable counterparty side. The internal alias sentence ("Teleglobe USA Inc. is referred to in this Subparagraph 18.1A as the 'Customer'") and the "Notwithstanding Subparagraph 18.1" opener are necessary in a multi-party agreement to identify the beneficiary and displace the 25-year lock-in, so they are not cosmetic extras.

Note (not a failure): "any amounts prepaid" is marginally broader than "prepaid fees" and, in a capital-contribution consortium, could be read to reach prepaid capital sums; if the counterparty pushes back, narrowing to "prepaid charges/fees" would keep the element intact without weakening our position.

Intent is preserved: no term is left undefined, no cross-reference dangles, and the retained sentence denying capital-cost credit is keyed expressly to Subparagraph 18.1, so it neither contradicts nor silently taxes a 18.1A withdrawal; 18.2's unanimous/90% mid-term mechanic and paragraph 23's for-cause default remedies survive untouched.
The drafter correctly declines to double-flag the capital-cost credit forfeiture, reserving it for the liquidated-damages rule.
